strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: existing deep-learning CT reconstruction methods overfit to fixed acquisition settings, and a unified model that handles varying sampling rates and output resolutions is valuable for clinical deployment.

The proposed CTO architecture is well-designed and physically grounded: DISCO operators applied in the native polar (θ, r) sinogram domain, joint spatial–frequency sinogram learning motivated by the Fourier slice theorem and FBP, and flipped circular padding that realizes the π-periodicity-with-flip symmetry. The rotational equivariance derivation in Supplementary Sec. A is clean and correct.

Comprehensive experiments: two datasets (C4KC-KiTS, AAPM abdomen), multiple sampling rates (9/18/36/72 views), multiple strong baselines spanning learning-free (FBP, SART), diffusion (DPS, ALD), and single-pass (DuDoTrans, GloReDi, unrolled CNN) methods, with full test-set results and qualitative comparisons across rates.

The unrolled CNN baseline with matched cascades/model size serves as a controlled ablation isolating the function-space (DISCO) contribution, and the ~4 dB PSNR gain over it supports the core claim that resolution-agnostic operator learning (not just capacity) drives the improvement.

Zero-shot super-resolution experiments in both image space (NOi, 256→512) and sinogram space (72→144 views) directly test the resolution-generalization claim without retraining, and the NO retains a consistent kernel-to-domain ratio while the CNN baseline degrades—good evidence for the central thesis.

Significant practical advantages demonstrated: ~500× faster inference than diffusion methods with higher PSNR, and no per-pattern tuning; ablations justify the rotational-equivariance padding (~0.8 dB) and the detector-axis FFT choice, consistent with the Fourier slice theorem argument.

Appropriate attribution: the paper is transparent that DISCO and UDNO build on prior work [22, 23], positioning its contribution as the CT-specific sinogram-space operator design and joint-domain unrolled formulation.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily architectural adaptation and integration rather than a new operator or learning principle: DISCO [23], UDNO [22] (already used for multi-pattern MRI), and unrolled networks [1] are all existing components; the contribution is their combination and CT-specific sinogram-space instantiation (polar coordinates, flipped circular padding). This is a solid but incremental contribution for an Algorithms/General paper.

The headline multi-rate generalization is partially trained-in: the single model is 'trained jointly over all sampling rates, with each rate being encountered equally during training.' Thus the >4 dB gains across rates partly reflect multi-task training rather than pure out-of-distribution generalization; only the super-resolution experiments are truly zero-shot. A zero-shot evaluation on an unseen sampling rate (e.g., 24 or 144 views for the main task) would substantially strengthen the claim.

The claim of inherent rotation equivariance is approximate: it holds up to quadrature error in the discrete DISCO implementation, and only the padding/symmetry handling is enforced—full SO(2)-equivariance of the whole unrolled pipeline (including image-domain NOi on a Cartesian grid) is not rigorously established. The language could be more precise.

2D parallel-beam/fan-beam slice reconstruction only; the fan/parallel geometry mismatch between training settings and real helical/cone-beam acquisition is not discussed, and no limited-angle or noisy-measurement experiments are included—both clinically important regimes. Extension to 3D is deferred to future work.

Reporting conventions raise some questions: the main Table 1 uses a 500-slice random subset (justified only for diffusion baselines, but the main table then omits diffusion for the full 10k set), and the super-resolution ground truth is bilinearly interpolated 512×512 images rather than actual high-resolution acquisitions, which may understate/overstate SR gains.

Some baselines may be under-tuned or under-trained (e.g., diffusion model trained for only 2,000 iterations; DuDoTrans/GloReDi trained for 100 epochs), making the 3–6 dB margins over them somewhat harder to interpret; the speed advantage over diffusion is expected by design (single-pass vs. iterative sampling).

RMSE values (e.g., ~53 HU at 18-view) are still far from clinical diagnostic quality, and no task-based evaluation (e.g., lesion detectability) or downstream-task validation is provided despite clinical deployment motivation; there is no societal-impact or clinical-validation discussion beyond generic motivation.
No statement about code or data release, which limits reproducibility of a system with many implementation-specific choices (kernel basis counts, radius cutoff, padding schemes).

strengths: Well-motivated problem: generalization across acquisition settings (view sampling rate and image resolution) is a genuine practical limitation of CNN-based CT reconstruction, and the paper articulates it clearly.

The proposed CTO framework is coherent: replacing CNN priors in unrolled networks with DISCO-based neural operators in both sinogram (polar coordinates) and image domains, with joint spatial–frequency sinogram learning inspired by FBP. The design rationale (Fourier slice theorem, π-periodicity-with-flip boundary conditions) is physically grounded and well explained.

Strong and consistent empirical gains: >4dB PSNR over a matched-size unrolled CNN across sampling rates, ~3dB over diffusion baselines (DPS/ALD) with at least 500x faster inference, on two datasets (C4KC-KiTS, AAPM low-dose abdomen), with full-test-set results in the supplementary.

Useful ablations: frequency-domain strategies (detector-axis FFT best), rotational equivariance/circular padding (+0.83 dB), and zero-shot super-resolution in both sinogram (144-view from 72-view training) and image space (512x512 from 256x256 training) directly probe the resolution/sampling-agnostic claims rather than only claiming them.

Appropriate attribution: DISCO [23], UDNO [22], unrolled networks [1], and baselines are clearly credited, and the supplementary provides implementation and baseline details supporting reproducibility.
Contribution type is effectively Applied/Systems (adapting an existing operator architecture to CT with CT-specific symmetries); assessed on that basis, the evidence adequately supports the claims.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core building blocks (DISCO, UDNO, unrolled optimization) are all borrowed, most notably from [22], which already applies UDNO/DISCO to unified cross-undersampling MRI reconstruction. The genuinely new elements are the polar-coordinate sinogram operator, flipped circular padding for the π-periodicity-with-flip identity, and the CT application itself—an incremental adaptation.

Evaluation is entirely on simulated sinograms (synthetic Radon/fan-beam transforms of 2D slices). There is no real scanner data, no 3D/cone-beam geometry, and no noise/metal-artifact regimes, which weakens the clinical deployment claims in the abstract and introduction.

The 'rotation-equivariant' claim is approximate: equivariance holds up to quadrature error and relies on padding rather than a strictly equivariant parameterization; only one ablation (24-view) supports it, and the claimed exact SO(2) equivariance in the supplementary is somewhat overstated relative to the implementation.

Sampling-rate generalization is trained jointly over all rates; the paper does not disentangle how much gain comes from function-space parameterization versus simply multi-rate training, and the CNN baseline's protocol under this joint training could be described more carefully.

Diffusion baselines are evaluated on only a 500-slice subset, and are omitted from the 10,000-slice kidney test set (Table 4); the headline '3dB over SOTA diffusion with 500x speedup' therefore rests on a reduced comparison, and diffusion baselines (DPS/ALD with a 2000-iteration EDM training) may not represent the strongest diffusion-based CT methods.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a paper whose main value is an implementation-oriented framework.
Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'Mathamatically', Fig. reference typos, some redundancy between Secs. 3 and 4), and the summary omits a frank discussion of the 2D-simulation limitation.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem in sparse-view CT: deployment requires a single model that generalizes across view-sampling rates and image resolutions, whereas most learned methods are tied to a fixed discretization.

The design is well-matched to the problem structure: the sinogram-space operator in polar coordinates with circular (flip-consistent) padding yields rotational equivariance, and the detector-axis frequency branch is grounded in the Fourier slice theorem and FBP intuition. The mathematical exposition of the symmetry (π-periodicity-with-flip) and its padding realization is clear and correct.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: two datasets (C4KC-KiTS kidney, AAPM abdomen), multiple view rates (9/18/36/72), diverse baselines spanning learning-free (FBP, SART), single-pass CNN/transformer (unrolled CNN, DuDoTrans, GloReDi), and diffusion (DPS, ALD); full-test-set results in supplementary strengthen credibility.

The unrolled-CNN baseline with matched cascades/channels serves as a controlled ablation isolating the function-space (DISCO) inductive bias from overall capacity, making the >4dB PSNR claim attributable to the architecture rather than model size.
Useful ablations: frequency-domain design variants (FFT along r vs θ vs 2D), rotational-equivariance padding (+0.83dB), and inference-time comparison (0.065s vs 30–50s for diffusion).

Zero-shot super-resolution experiments in both image space (256→512) and sinogram space (72→144 views) directly test the central resolution-agnostic claim rather than only in-distribution performance.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core components (DISCO convolutions, UDNO, unrolled data-consistency cascades) are adopted from prior work [22, 23]; the contribution is primarily an application/systems adaptation to CT (polar-coordinate operator, flipped circular padding, FFT-along-r branch). The paper is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General, which tempers the assessment of originality.

The diffusion baselines appear potentially undertrained (only 2,000 iterations for a 65M-parameter EDM model vs. many more for other baselines), which casts doubt on the headline claims of '>3dB gain and 500× speedup over state-of-the-art diffusion'; moreover, diffusion metrics are computed on a random 500-slice subset, and diffusion models are dropped from the largest test set, weakening the strongest comparative claims.

Generality claims are only partially substantiated: 'resolution-agnostic' is tested mainly via zero-shot 256→512 super-resolution with bilinearly interpolated ground truth (a weak reference), and 2D only. Both geometries (parallel/fan-beam) and both datasets are 2D; no 3D, cone-beam, or real scanner sinograms are evaluated, limiting clinical deployability claims.

Training protocol fairness is not fully clarified: CTO is trained jointly across all sampling rates, but it is not stated whether unrolled-CNN and other baselines receive the same joint multi-rate training or per-rate training; this materially affects the interpretation of the multi-rate comparisons.

Dataset construction raises slice-correlation concerns: 33,000 training slices from only 170 patients with central-slice-heavy sampling implies highly correlated training data, and test slices from held-out patients may still overlap anatomically; patient-level generalization would be a stronger test.

Rotation-equivariance gains are modest (0.83dB at a single 24-view setting) and the equivariance is exact only up to quadrature error; quantitative evaluation over rotated inputs (beyond the qualitative Fig. 3c) is not provided.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned; several key results (Supplementary Tables 3–5, Fig. 7) are only in the supplementary, and the PSNR/SSIM are reported pre-HU-conversion while RMSE is post-conversion, which complicates comparison with prior CT literature.

Important practical aspects are deferred to future work: limited-angle geometries, metal artifacts, noise realism, and dose-dependent nonuniform sampling are unaddressed, and the related work cites cross-view generalization diffusion [43] without comparing against it.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: discretization/sampling-rate dependence of learning-based CT reconstruction is a real practical limitation, and the paper articulates it precisely with supporting evidence (Table 2a).

Sound, physics-informed design: the sinogram-space operator NOs in polar (θ,r) coordinates with flipped-circular padding correctly encodes the π-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of the Radon transform, and the rotation-equivariance argument is formalized cleanly in Supp. Sec. A. The frequency branch is well justified via the Fourier slice theorem and its connection to FBP ramp filtering.

Extensive and largely fair experimental evidence: three datasets (AAPM, KiTS, LIDC-IDRI), a broad baseline set (classical, single-pass, unrolled, diffusion), matched multi-rate training for all methods, single-rate ablation (Supp. Table 8) showing CTO still wins, matched-parameter CNN ablation (Supp. Table 11) isolating the effect of continuous kernels, and thorough ablations (NOs/NOi branches, circular padding, FFT variants, DISCO hyperparameters).

Practically meaningful results: consistent ~3 dB PSNR gains over the matched unrolled CNN, 500× faster inference than diffusion with comparable or better quality, and zero-shot generalization to unseen resolutions and noisy sinograms.
Good reproducibility: detailed architecture, training, and baseline re-implementation details in the supplementary; code release is promised.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic novelty is moderate: DISCO kernels, unrolled dual-domain design, and the neural-operator concept are all adopted from prior work; the contribution is primarily a careful application/adaptation (polar-coordinate extension, rotation-equivariant padding, frequency branch) rather than a new operator class. The paper acknowledges this, but reviewers should calibrate expectations accordingly.

Evaluation is limited to simulated 2D parallel-/fan-beam geometries at a fixed 256×256 resolution; no real scanner data, cone-beam, or 3D acquisitions. Given the strong clinical-practice motivation, the gap between the simulated setting and actual clinical deployment is a nontrivial limitation.

Baselines were retrained under a multi-rate protocol and therefore show numbers below their originally published results; although a single-rate ablation (Supp. Table 8) mitigates this concern, the main table does not directly establish superiority over published SOTA numbers under the original protocols.

Zero-shot super-resolution is evaluated against bilinearly upsampled 'ground truth,' which weakens the interpretation of the reported SR gains; a natively acquired higher-resolution evaluation would be more convincing.

Some claims are stated a bit strongly for the evidence (e.g., 'first NO for sparse-view CT' rests on an exhaustive-literature assumption), and the manuscript has minor polish issues (abstract's code URL is incomplete; several key quantitative results deferred to the supplementary).

Only MSE training loss is used; perceptual/adversarial alternatives or data-consistency-aware losses are not explored, so it is unclear whether the gains come from the operator formulation or partially from favorable regularization under multi-rate training.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: a single model that generalizes across sampling rates and image resolutions addresses a genuine limitation of existing sparse-view CT methods that are discretization-bound.

Comprehensive and generally fair experimental evaluation: multi-rate co-training is applied to all baselines so that gains cannot be attributed to a training-data advantage; comparisons include learning-free, single-pass, unrolled, and diffusion baselines on three datasets (AAPM, KiTS, LIDC-IDRI), plus noisy-sinogram and cross-dataset OOD tests.

Thoughtful CT-specific design: polar-coordinate extension of DISCO with flipped circular padding correctly exploits the sinogram symmetries (theta-shift and pi-periodicity-with-flip), supported by a short equivariance derivation in the supplement and an ablation (+0.83 dB).

Useful efficiency analysis: inference-time equivalence of DISCO and CNN convolutions is demonstrated with matched-parameter and matched-architecture ablations (Table 11), and the 500x speedup over diffusion baselines is practically relevant.
Extensive ablations (NOs/NOi branches, FFT placement, kernel hyperparameters, circular padding) that validate each design decision.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core building block (DISCO), the U-shaped block (UDNO), and the unrolled dual-domain cascades are all adopted from prior work [25,34,3]. The contribution is primarily an application-level adaptation (polar coordinates, circular padding, Fourier branch along r), which weakens the claim of a fundamentally new method; this is closer to an Applied/Systems contribution than a new algorithm.

Simulation-only, 2D evaluation: all experiments use parallel/fan-beam geometry with synthetic subsampling from 720-view sinograms at 256x256. There is no real scanner data, no cone-beam or 3D volume evaluation, and no perceptual/task-level (e.g., segmentation or reader) assessment, which limits the clinical significance claims; the authors acknowledge this only in the summary.

Headline gains need careful interpretation: the abstract claims >3.4 dB over CNNs and >3 dB over diffusion, but in the multi-rate setting the CNN baseline was also trained with multi-rate data, and Table 8 shows single-rate training yields larger margins for CTO; the comparison regime differs from how baselines were originally published, and the paper only partially isolates the effect.

Some substantive evidence is deferred to the supplementary material (Kidney full-set results, 9-view results, OOD details, complexity analysis), and the code-release URL in the abstract is incomplete ('available at .'), which harms reproducibility as submitted.

The rotation-equivariance claim is technically a shift-equivariance along the theta axis with a flip at the boundary; calling it rotational equivariance is accurate only through the Radon-duality argument, and the empirical validation (Fig. 3c, Table 5) is limited to visual checks and a single-rate ablation.

Training uses only an MSE loss with no perceptual or data-consistency fine-tuning alternatives explored; at very sparse rates (9 views), the absolute PSNR (~27.6 dB) suggests the method may still fall short of clinically usable quality, yet no failure analysis is provided.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clinically relevant limitation of learning-based CT reconstruction: discretization/sampling-rate overfitting. Framing sparse-view CT reconstruction as learning a map between function spaces via neural operators is a well-motivated and, to the best of the authors' knowledge, first-of-its-kind application for SVCT, giving the work clear conceptual novelty beyond a straightforward architectural swap.

The technical design is thoughtful and well-grounded in CT physics: extending DISCO convolutions from Cartesian to polar (theta, r) sinogram coordinates, the flipped-circular padding scheme that respects the pi-periodicity-with-flip identity (Eq. 8), and the dual-branch NO_s (spatial + detector-axis Fourier) with a Fourier-slice-theorem justification are all sensible and carefully reasoned contributions rather than ad hoc choices.

The experimental evidence is extensive and fairly designed: multi-rate co-training for ALL baselines (a fair protocol that the authors honestly note differs from baselines' original single-rate training), two primary datasets (AAPM, KiTS) plus a third (LIDC-IDRI), four sampling rates, zero-shot super-resolution in both image and sinogram domains, OOD experiments (noise, cross-dataset transfer), and thorough ablations (NO_s vs NO_i, frequency-domain variants, circular padding, kernel hyperparameters, matched-parameter CNN comparison).

The efficiency claims are credible and well-supported: 500x faster inference than diffusion methods with ~3 dB gain (Table 2b), plus a detailed complexity analysis (Supp. D) showing DISCO incurs no inference-time overhead over CNNs and only modest training-time cost, with a matched-FLOP/matched-parameter comparison isolating the benefit of continuous kernel parameterization (Table 11, 2.43 dB at identical cost).
The code release claim and detailed supplementary (baseline implementations, hyperparameter search methodology) support reproducibility.

Contribution type: while no type is declared and the default would be Algorithms/General, the work is best read as an Applied/Systems contribution (a novel application/system of neural operators to CT). Judged under that lens, the evidence is appropriately strong: the contribution does not need new operator theory, and the careful adaptation of DISCO plus the equivariance/padding design constitutes sufficient methodological novelty.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic machinery (DISCO kernels, U-shaped blocks, unrolled optimization, dual-domain refinement, Fourier-domain priors) is largely borrowed from prior work. The novelty lies in the composition and the polar/equivariance adaptation; while legitimate, a reviewer could argue the paper is primarily an application paper, and the theoretical claims (e.g., discretization-convergence) are inherited from [34] rather than newly established for this setting.

Scope is limited to 2D parallel- and fan-beam geometries at 256x256 resolution. Clinically dominant cone-beam and helical 3D acquisition are not addressed, which tempers the clinical-impact narrative; the authors acknowledge this as future work, but it bounds the practical significance of the resolution-agnostic claim (only zero-shot upsampling to 512x512 is demonstrated).

Some quantitative claims rest on partially reduced evaluations: diffusion comparisons use a 500-slice subset of the kidney test set due to cost, and some ablations (e.g., rotational equivariance, Table 5) are on a single 24-view setting; broader evaluation would strengthen the evidence.

A fair concern about the headline gains: baselines retrained under multi-rate co-training perform substantially below their originally published numbers, so the large margins (e.g., ~6 dB over DPS) partly reflect the multi-rate protocol rather than head-to-head single-rate superiority. The authors handle this honestly (and report single-rate training in Supp. Table 8, where CTO still wins), but the abstract's phrasing could be read as overclaiming against prior SOTA as reported.

No perceptual/downstream-task evaluation (e.g., lesion detectability, segmentation performance on reconstructions) and no real-scanner or physics-realistic noise data beyond simulated Poisson noise at one dose level; PSNR/SSIM/RMSE alone may not fully substantiate clinical applicability claims.

Some presentation issues: the abstract's code link is a dangling placeholder, and key implementation choices (e.g., radius cutoff 0.02, 720-view ground-truth generation) are deferred to the supplement, which slightly impedes readability of the main text.
